claims.claim_vi: The source body is four teaser lines: HTTPS protects data from eavesdroppers and breaches and encryption plus digital certificates make an 'impregnable shield'; the SSL handshake is the cryptographic exchange of keys and negotiation; data travels through an encrypted 'tunnel'; and a side remark about HTML and why it is called hyper text. Its explanatory image was not used.

claims.claim_vi: MDN: TLS secures a connection in three ways, encryption, integrity (an attacker cannot secretly modify data in transit) and authentication (on the web servers usually authenticate themselves to clients, clients usually do not); HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.
claims.verified_by: Read from the file at the pinned mdn/content commit (fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com).

claims.claim_vi: MDN: the handshake sets security parameters: the two sides agree on the TLS version and the cipher suite, optionally authenticate each other (server authentication is fundamental on the web), and agree on a secret key; after the handshake they use the secret key to encrypt and decrypt all messages including HTTP headers and bodies.
claims.verified_by: Read from the file at the pinned mdn/content commit.

claims.claim_vi: MDN glossary: TLS was formerly known as SSL; SSL was the old standard and has been superseded by TLS; HTTPS is an encrypted version of HTTP that uses TLS to encrypt all communication between client and server.
claims.verified_by: Read the glossary entries tls, ssl and https at the pinned mdn/content commit.

claims.claim_vi: MDN glossary: symmetric-key cryptography uses the same key for encryption and decryption and is highly efficient so it can encrypt large amounts of data; a cipher suite is a combination of key exchange algorithm, authentication method, bulk encryption cipher and message authentication code which client and server must agree on before communicating securely.
claims.verified_by: Read the glossary entries symmetric-key_cryptography and cipher_suite at the pinned mdn/content commit.

claims.claim_vi: OpenSSL guide: TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 are the most commonly deployed versions; TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are formally deprecated; TLS acts as a security layer over a lower-level transport, typically TCP; OpenSSL names contain SSL for historical reasons.

claims.verified_by: Read from the file at the pinned openssl/openssl commit.

claims.claim_vi: OpenSSL guide: the client sends ClientHello and the server answers ServerHello; the handshake is complete once an endpoint has sent and received a Finished message; in TLS 1.3 the server always sends its Finished before the client.
claims.verified_by: Read from the file at the pinned openssl/openssl commit.

claims.claim_vi: OpenSSL guide: the server sends a certificate containing its DNS name and public key and proves it knows the matching private key by signing a message; a certificate authority verifies the information in the certificate; the client must check that the name in the certificate matches the name it connected to; s_client is a testing tool that continues after a verification error.

claims.claim_vi: openssl-s_client manual: -servername sets the SNI extension in the ClientHello; -msg shows protocol messages and -trace a verbose trace; -verify_return_error turns on server certificate verification and returns errors instead of continuing (typically aborting the handshake); -keylogfile appends TLS secrets to a file. openssl-s_server manual: -www answers with a status page. openssl-req manual: -x509 outputs a self-signed test certificate.
claims.verified_by: Read the s_client, s_server and req manual sources at the pinned openssl/openssl commit; the -tls1_2/-tls1_3 version options come from a template in the s_client file and were exercised by running them.

claims.claim_vi: Observed TLS 1.3 handshake (TLSv1.3, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, key exchange group x25519, ECDSA P-256 certificate): the client sent ClientHello with server_name localhost, a supported_groups list and a key_share for x25519; the server sent ServerHello (key_share x25519), a 1-byte ChangeCipherSpec record, and four records of outer type ApplicationData that s_client printed as EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished; the client sent ChangeCipherSpec, Finished and then the 35-byte HTTP request record; the server then sent two 250-byte records printed as NewSessionTicket, a 4348-byte response record and an encrypted close alert.
claims.section: Đọc hình, khung 2 và 3; Xem sâu hơn
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; Observed by running openssl 3.0.13 (s_server and s_client on 127.0.0.1 with a throw-away self-signed certificate) and a small Python relay that recorded the bytes; one or a few runs per configuration on the authoring machine; the server was killed afterwards. Commands: s_client -tls1_3 -trace (and -msg), plus the relay's record log.

claims.claim_vi: Observed TLS 1.2 handshake (TLSv1.2, ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384, ephemeral key x25519): ClientHello; ServerHello, Certificate, ServerKeyExchange (key exchange value with signature) and ServerHelloDone; ClientKeyExchange, ChangeCipherSpec, Finished; NewSessionTicket, ChangeCipherSpec, Finished; then application data. The 413-byte certificate and the string localhost appeared in clear in the server's bytes. The Finished records have outer type Handshake and a length of 40 bytes; that they are encrypted is an inference from their position after ChangeCipherSpec, not a decryption.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; Observed by running openssl 3.0.13 (s_server and s_client on 127.0.0.1 with a throw-away self-signed certificate) and a small Python relay that recorded the bytes; one or a few runs per configuration on the authoring machine; the server was killed afterwards. Commands: s_client -tls1_2 -trace, plus the relay's record log and a byte search.

claims.claim_vi: Inferred from the order of messages in the two runs: in TLS 1.3 the client sends its HTTP request after one reply flight from the server, in TLS 1.2 after two.
claims.verified_by: Counted from the recorded message order of the runs; not timed.

claims.claim_vi: Observed on the recorded bytes: with plain HTTP (a Python http.server behind the relay) the request line GET / HTTP/1.0, the response status and the response text appeared in clear; with TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 the request line, the response status and the response text were not found in the recorded bytes; in TLS 1.3 the certificate (413 bytes) was not found while in TLS 1.2 it was; the string localhost was found in the bytes the client sent in both TLS versions (the server name in the ClientHello); the record headers show each record's length (e.g. 4348 bytes for the response in TLS 1.3).

claims.claim_vi: Observed integrity: changing one bit of the last byte of the server's response record on the wire made s_client report 'decryption failed or bad record mac' (TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2) and print no response page; with plain HTTP the same one-bit change was accepted and the client printed 'iello' instead of 'hello'.

claims.claim_vi: Observed certificate checks: s_client -verify_return_error without a trusted CA printed 'self-signed certificate' and aborted (exit code 1); with -CAfile set to the throw-away certificate but -verify_hostname set to another name it printed 'hostname mismatch' and aborted; without -verify_return_error and without -CAfile it printed the self-signed error but still connected, received the page, and the request line was not found on the wire (the channel was still encrypted without trusting the certificate). Without a version option s_client and s_server negotiated TLS 1.3.

claims.claim_vi: Each side combines the other's public key share with its own secret part to compute the same shared secret, and an eavesdropper who has only the two public shares cannot recompute it (property of the key exchange; not proved in the lesson).
claims.verified_by: Author's general knowledge; not checked against a source or an experiment here. Only the observation that the secrets do not appear on the wire was checked (see the key log claim).

claims.claim_vi: The server's IP address cannot be hidden because packets need a destination address; a fraudulent site with its own domain can usually still obtain a certificate for that domain; what a server does with data after decrypting it is outside HTTPS.
claims.verified_by: Author's general knowledge; not checked against a source or an experiment here.

claims.claim_vi: In TLS 1.3 the cipher suite name (TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384) covers the data encryption and hash only, while the key exchange group and signature algorithms are separate extensions (supported_groups, signature_algorithms were printed in the ClientHello); in TLS 1.2 the name includes the key exchange and authentication parts (ECDHE-ECDSA-...).
claims.verified_by: The names and the extensions were observed in the -trace output; Observed by running openssl 3.0.13 (s_server and s_client on 127.0.0.1 with a throw-away self-signed certificate) and a small Python relay that recorded the bytes; one or a few runs per configuration on the authoring machine; the server was killed afterwards. Reading AES-256-GCM as the data encryption and SHA384 as the hash is the author's general knowledge.

design_notes_vi: Bốn khung xếp dọc: ba thứ HTTPS thêm vào, hai khung trình tự cho bắt tay TLS 1.3 rút gọn (tách đôi để vừa một slide), và một khung nhớ các giới hạn. Không dùng ảnh nguồn.
source_deviations: The source body is only four teaser lines with the explanation in an image; the lesson writes its own explanation and does not use the image.
The source calls the exchange an 'SSL handshake'; the lesson calls it a TLS handshake because SSL is the old name and TLS 1.3 or 1.2 is what runs (the tools still print 'SSL').

The source says HTTPS safeguards data from 'eavesdroppers and breaches' and that encryption and certificates form an 'impregnable shield'; the lesson says HTTPS protects data in transit only, the server still sees the data, and the server name and record lengths stay visible.

The source presents digital certificates next to encryption as what creates the shield; the run showed encryption still works when the certificate is not trusted, so the lesson says the key exchange gives the encryption and the certificate is for knowing who the server is.

The source speaks of an encrypted 'tunnel'; the lesson says the TLS records travel on the same TCP connection (OpenSSL guide: a security layer over a lower-level transport) and not in a separate channel.
The source's aside on HTML and why it is called hyper text has no bearing on encryption; the lesson says so in one sentence in the deep-dive section.
